questions.text: DBMS stands for
questions.explanation: A Database Management System is software that stores, retrieves and manages data in databases.

questions.text: Which level of the three-schema architecture describes how data is physically stored?
questions.explanation: The internal (physical) level describes storage structures; the conceptual level describes the whole logical database.

questions.text: Physical data independence means
options: changing the physical storage does not require changing the conceptual schema
questions.explanation: Programs and the logical schema stay the same when storage structures or indexes change.

questions.text: In an ER diagram, an entity set is drawn as a
questions.explanation: Rectangles are entity sets, diamonds relationships, and ellipses attributes.

questions.text: A weak entity set is one that
options: cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone
questions.explanation: A weak entity depends on an identifying owner entity and has only a partial key.

questions.text: A multivalued attribute in an ER diagram is shown as
questions.explanation: Double ellipses mark multivalued attributes; dashed ellipses mark derived attributes.

questions.text: A primary key is
options: a minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row and is not null
questions.explanation: The chosen candidate key that identifies each tuple uniquely; its values cannot be null.

questions.text: A foreign key
options: uniquely identifies a row in its own table
refers to the primary key of another (or the same) table
questions.explanation: A foreign key enforces referential integrity by matching a key in the referenced table.

questions.text: A candidate key is
options: any superset of the primary key
questions.explanation: A candidate key is a superkey from which no attribute can be removed; one is chosen as the primary key.

questions.text: Which relational algebra operation selects rows that satisfy a condition?
questions.explanation: σ condition (R) keeps the tuples of R that satisfy the condition; π keeps columns.

questions.text: The projection operation (π) in relational algebra
options: selects columns and removes duplicate rows
questions.explanation: π attribute-list (R) returns only the listed attributes, as a set without duplicates.

questions.text: A natural join of R and S
options: pairs every row of R with every row of S
joins on all attributes with the same name and keeps one copy of them
questions.explanation: It equates the common attributes and removes the duplicate columns from the result.

questions.text: Which SQL command is part of the Data Definition Language (DDL)?
questions.explanation: DDL commands define structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.

questions.text: Which SQL command is part of DML?
questions.explanation: DML commands change data: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (and SELECT is often grouped with them).

questions.text: GRANT and REVOKE belong to
questions.explanation: Data Control Language manages privileges.

questions.text: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT belong to
questions.explanation: Transaction Control Language ends or undoes transactions.

questions.text: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups using aggregates.

questions.text: Which aggregate function ignores NULL values and counts only non-null entries in a column?
questions.explanation: COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row.

questions.text: What does DELETE FROM student; do?
options: Removes all rows but keeps the table
questions.explanation: DELETE without WHERE removes every row; the table structure remains.

questions.text: How does TRUNCATE differ from DELETE?
options: TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly as DDL and cannot use WHERE
questions.explanation: TRUNCATE is DDL that deallocates all rows at once; DELETE is DML and can filter with WHERE.

questions.text: Which join returns all rows of the left table and matching rows of the right table?
questions.explanation: A left outer join keeps unmatched left rows, filling the right columns with NULL.

questions.text: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a SELECT result?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT returns each different row once.

questions.text: Which operator checks for a pattern in a string column?
questions.explanation: LIKE with % and _ wildcards matches patterns, e.g. name LIKE 'A%'.

questions.text: A view in SQL is
options: a physical copy of a table
a stored query that acts as a virtual table
questions.explanation: A view stores a SELECT; querying the view runs it against the base tables.

questions.text: A trigger is
options: a stored procedure called by the user
code run automatically when an event such as INSERT happens on a table
questions.explanation: Triggers fire before or after INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table.

questions.text: Normalisation is mainly used to
questions.explanation: Decomposing relations by functional dependencies removes redundancy and anomalies.

questions.text: A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) if
options: it has a primary key of one column
questions.explanation: 1NF forbids repeating groups and multivalued attributes in a cell.

questions.text: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and
options: has no partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on a candidate key
questions.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key.

questions.text: A relation is in 3NF if it is in 2NF and
options: has no transitive dependency of non-prime attributes on a key
questions.explanation: 3NF removes non-key attributes that depend on other non-key attributes.

questions.text: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that
options: every determinant is a candidate key
questions.explanation: For every non-trivial FD X → Y, X must be a superkey.

questions.text: Given R(A, B, C) with A → B and B → C, what is the key and the highest normal form?
questions.explanation: A determines B and C, so A is the key; B → C is a transitive dependency, so R is in 2NF but not 3NF.

questions.text: A functional dependency X → Y means
options: each value of X is associated with exactly one value of Y
X and Y are both keys
questions.explanation: Two tuples that agree on X must agree on Y.

questions.text: A lossless-join decomposition of R into R1 and R2 requires that
options: R1 ∩ R2 is a key of R1 or of R2
R1 and R2 have the same attributes
questions.explanation: If the common attributes determine all of R1 or all of R2, joining them back gives exactly R.

questions.text: ACID stands for
questions.explanation: The four properties every transaction must satisfy.

questions.text: Atomicity of a transaction means
options: either all of its operations happen or none do
questions.explanation: A partially done transaction is rolled back, so it is all or nothing.

questions.text: Durability means
options: the committed changes survive system failures
questions.explanation: Once committed, changes persist, usually through the log.

questions.text: A schedule is conflict serializable if
options: it can be turned into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting operations
it runs transactions at the same time
questions.explanation: This is checked with a precedence graph: the schedule is conflict serializable if the graph has no cycle.

questions.text: In two-phase locking (2PL), a transaction
options: releases all locks before acquiring any
acquires all its locks before it releases any
questions.explanation: The growing phase only acquires locks and the shrinking phase only releases them, which ensures serializability.

questions.text: A deadlock happens when
options: two or more transactions each wait for a lock held by the other
questions.explanation: Each transaction waits for the others in a cycle, so none can go on.

questions.text: Which problem occurs when a transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed?
questions.explanation: Reading uncommitted data is a dirty read; if the writer rolls back, the reader used a value that never existed.

questions.text: In the write-ahead logging (WAL) rule,
options: data pages are written before the log
the log record of a change is written to stable storage before the changed data page
questions.explanation: Writing the log first makes it possible to undo or redo changes after a crash.

questions.text: Which index structure is used by most relational databases for range queries?
questions.explanation: B+ tree leaves are sorted and linked, so ranges are read in order.

questions.text: A clustered index
options: is stored separately from the data in any order
determines the physical order of the rows in the table
can exist many times on one table
questions.explanation: Rows are stored in the order of the clustered index key, so there can be only one.

questions.text: A hash index is best for
options: equality lookups such as WHERE id = 7
questions.explanation: Hashing finds a key's bucket directly but keeps no order, so ranges need a scan.

questions.text: Which SQL constraint makes sure a column never holds NULL?
questions.explanation: NOT NULL rejects any row without a value in that column.
